title: Ten Virgins, the Talents, and the Sheep and Goats
summary: Jesus completes his teaching on the Mount of Olives with three pictures of readiness for his return. Ten young women wait for a bridegroom, and only those with oil enough enter the feast; three servants are entrusted with their master's money, and the one who buried his is condemned; and the Son of Man, enthroned as king, separates the nations as a shepherd separates sheep from goats, judging them by how they treated the least of his brothers.
story: Chapter 24 ended with the call to keep watch because no one knows the day or hour, and with a parable about a faithful and a wicked servant. Chapter 25 continues the same discourse without a break. The first two parables develop the two sides of readiness: being prepared for a long delay, and working faithfully with what has been entrusted. The chapter closes with a scene of final judgment that concludes Jesus' teaching in Matthew. In the next verse, 26:1, Matthew signals that Jesus has finished all these sayings, and the passion begins. The king who will judge the nations is about to be judged by them.
historical:
The chapter continues the same occasion as chapter 24, a few days before Passover, probably around AD 30 or 33, on the Mount of Olives across from the temple. Its setting in history is less a particular event than the situation Jesus foresees for his followers: a long interval between his departure and his return, in which some will grow careless and others will give up. Matthew's first readers, writing or reading after decades had passed, knew that interval firsthand. The parables of the delayed bridegroom and the master who returns after a long time (verse 19) speak directly to a church that had to learn to wait without losing heart.

The talent was the largest unit of money in common use. It was a weight of silver, reckoned at about six thousand denarii, and since a denarius was a day's wage for a laborer (20:2), one talent was roughly twenty years of work. Even the servant with one talent held a fortune. Burying valuables was a recognized way of keeping them safe in a world without secure banks, and Jewish law later treated burial as a responsible form of safekeeping, which makes the master's verdict all the sharper: caution was not the virtue he wanted.
cultural:
Village weddings followed a familiar pattern. The bridegroom went to the bride's family home, and after negotiations and celebration he brought her in procession to his own house, often at night, where the wedding feast took place. Friends of the bride waited to join the procession with lights. The lamps may have been small clay oil lamps or torches made of rags soaked in oil on a stick, which needed refueling for a long night; interpreters disagree which is meant. Either way, running out of oil meant missing the procession, and once the door of the house was shut the feast was closed. Delays in the bridegroom's arrival were common.

In the judgment scene, a Palestinian shepherd often grazed sheep and goats together in mixed flocks and separated them when needed, a scene every hearer would have watched. The right hand was the place of honor and favor. Care for the hungry, the stranger, the sick, and the prisoner was a well-established duty in Jewish piety. Prisoners in the ancient world often depended on friends and family for food and clothing, so visiting them was not a courtesy but a lifeline, and it could be dangerous to be associated with them.
literary: The chapter contains two parables and a judgment scene, all bound to the refrain of chapter 24: the master or bridegroom comes at an unexpected time. The ten virgins and the talents both divide characters into the ready and the unready, and both end with exclusion (a shut door, outer darkness). The judgment scene is not strictly a parable, though it contains a simile (the shepherd). It is built on repetition: the list of six needs is spoken four times, by the king and by each group in reply, with small variations. The repetition slows the reader and makes the surprise of both groups the heart of the scene: neither the righteous nor the condemned knew that they had been dealing with the king.

outline.t: The parable of the ten virgins
The Son of Man judges the nations

doctrines.note: Every person and nation will stand before the Son of Man, and the judgment is final, issuing in eternal life or eternal punishment. The standard is how people treated the king in the persons of the least.

The righteous are invited to inherit a kingdom prepared for them from the foundation of the world. God's purpose for his people was settled before history began, and the end of the story is joy, a feast, and the master's welcome.

Readiness is not anxious date setting but steady faithfulness: oil kept in store, entrusted gifts put to work, and mercy shown to the needy. The servant who buried his talent failed because he misjudged his master's character.

words.note: Talanton, talent, a large weight of silver or gold used as a unit of money. The English word talent, meaning a natural gift, comes from this parable. In the story itself it is money, standing for whatever the master entrusts, which includes gifts but also the gospel, opportunities, and responsibilities.

Elachistos, least or smallest. Jesus identifies himself with the least of these brothers of his. Elsewhere in Matthew he calls his disciples his brothers (12:49-50, 28:10) and speaks of little ones who belong to him (10:42), which bears on the debate over who these people are.

Aionios, eternal, literally belonging to the age, meaning the age to come. The same word describes both eternal punishment and eternal life in verse 46, so the two destinies are given matching weight. It speaks of the quality of the coming age and of its lasting character.

Nymphios, bridegroom. Jesus used the word of himself earlier (9:15), drawing on the Old Testament picture of God as Israel's husband. In the parable the long-awaited bridegroom stands for the Son of Man at his coming.

christ: Here Jesus presents himself as the bridegroom, the master who entrusts his goods and returns, and above all as the Son of Man seated on his glorious throne, the King who judges all the nations. This picture draws on Daniel 7, where the Son of Man receives dominion over all peoples, and on the Old Testament's portrait of God as shepherd and judge (Ezekiel 34:17). Yet the King identifies himself with the hungry, the stranger, and the prisoner. Within days he will be stripped, bound, and imprisoned himself. The judge of all is the one who took the place of the least, and his people meet him in the needy.

hard.q: Who are the least of these brothers, and does this passage teach that we are saved by good deeds?
hard.a:
There are two main readings of the brothers. Many interpreters, noting that Jesus calls his disciples his brothers and speaks of his little ones elsewhere in Matthew (10:40-42), think the least are his followers, especially needy messengers of the gospel, so that the nations are judged by how they received Christ's people. Many others take the least to be any person in need, Christian or not, since the list of needs is universal and the scene is about all nations. Both readings have strong defenders, and both make care for the vulnerable a mark of belonging to the king.

On salvation, the passage does not teach that people earn eternal life by works. The righteous are surprised by their reward, which is an inheritance prepared for them, not wages. The judgment reveals what kind of people they are; the deeds are evidence of a life already turned toward Christ, as Jesus said a tree is known by its fruit (12:33). The church's confession that salvation is by grace through faith stands alongside this passage's warning that faith which never feeds the hungry or visits the prisoner is not the faith that saves.

questions: The foolish virgins could not borrow oil at the last minute. What parts of readiness for God can no one else supply for you?
The third servant said he was afraid because he thought his master was hard. How does what you believe about God's character shape what you do with what he has given you?
Neither group in the judgment scene knew they were serving or ignoring the king. Who are the least in your city or church, and how would you treat them if you saw Christ in them?
